script.opening: (Angry, upset, talking fast.) "I found a bag of cannabis in Jacob's room this morning and I am beside myself. I want you to get him in and drug-test him, and frankly I want to know what he's been telling you in his appointments, because I'm his mother and I have a right to know. Can you call him in and put the fear of God into him? I don't know what else to do — you have to fix this."

facts.text: You are Karen, 42, Jacob's mother. Jacob is 16, in Year 12 at the local sixth form. He does not know you are ringing. "He'd go mad if he knew I'd called you."
If asked: "A small plastic bag of what I'm pretty sure is weed, in his hoodie pocket. And some rolling papers." No pills, powders, scales or large amounts of cash that you have seen.
"I don't actually know. His room smells of it some weekends. I think it's been going on since the summer." You have not seen him obviously high on school days.

Grades have dipped a bit this term; he is "moodier" and spends more time in his room, but he still goes to college, still plays football on Saturdays and still eats with you. He has never talked about harming himself that you know of. No police involvement, no new older friends, no unexplained phones, money or trips away.

facts.topic: The divorce (only if asked how things are at home)
facts.text: "His dad and I split up in the spring. It was horrible. He moved out in May." Jacob sees his dad every other weekend. You feel Jacob blames you.

facts.topic: How YOU are (only if the doctor asks about you)
facts.text: You are not sleeping well, you cry most evenings, you feel you are "losing him" and "failing as a mum". You are not suicidal and have no thoughts of harming yourself. You have not told anyone how bad things feel. You drink "a glass of wine most nights, maybe two".
No significant medical history. No regular medication. You work part-time as a school administrator.

The cannabis has become the focus for everything you feel about the divorce and losing control. Do NOT volunteer this. If the doctor asks warmly how YOU are coping, soften, become tearful and say: "Honestly? I feel like I'm failing at everything at the moment."

Start angry and demanding. If the doctor simply says "I can't tell you anything" and stops there, get angrier: "So you're just going to do nothing?" If they acknowledge how frightening this is BEFORE explaining confidentiality, calm down and listen. Accept the boundary if it is explained kindly with reasons, and if you are given something practical to do (how to talk to Jacob, where to get support, how he can see a doctor himself).

ice.ideas: "He's 16, I'm his mother — I should be able to know what he's told you, and you should be able to test him and sort him out."
ice.concerns: "I'm terrified he's going down a bad road and I've lost control of him." Underneath (only if asked about you): since the divorce you feel you are failing as a parent and you are struggling yourself.
ice.expectations: "I want him called in, drug-tested and scared straight, and I want to know what's in his notes." You will settle for a clear explanation, practical help to get Jacob to engage, and someone noticing that you are struggling too.

cues: "I have a right to know what he tells you." — say near the start; push back once if the doctor refuses without explaining why.
"I don't know what else to do — you have to fix this." — say with your voice breaking; this is your distress showing.
"Ever since his dad left..." — let this slip mid-way and trail off; expand only if the doctor picks it up.

checkpoints.text: Holds the CONFIDENTIALITY and CONSENT boundary correctly and kindly: cannot disclose a 16-year-old’s records to a parent (GMC 0–18 years; GMC Confidentiality 2017), cannot assess/treat or drug-test an absent young person on demand, and cannot act without his consent (at 16 he can consent to treatment under the Family Law Reform Act 1969, s8, and is presumed to have capacity under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 — Gillick competence is the test for under-16s, and the Fraser guidelines apply only to contraception advice) — explaining the reasons (his rights, and that confidentiality is what keeps young people coming for help)

Conducts a proportionate RISK/SAFEGUARDING screen via the mother: nature/escalation of use, other substances, mental-health change, school, signs of exploitation/county lines, risk to self/others — and recognises what WOULD justify safeguarding action (a genuine risk of significant harm, Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026; disclosure without consent only to protect him or others from a risk of death or serious harm, GMC Confidentiality 2017) versus what does not

Offers what CAN be done: general information about cannabis and adolescents, encouraging and facilitating Jacob to attend himself (confidentially), and signposting to young-people’s substance services (and FRANK for information) and parenting/family support (NICE NG64: prevention aimed at young people most at risk, with skills training for families) — turning a refused demand into constructive help

Addresses the mother’s OWN needs (the hidden agenda): explores the divorce, her sense of failing/losing control, and her mood/coping — recognising the caller is the person in front of you and may need support in her own right

Avoids being drawn into harmful actions: declines to "scare him straight", covert drug-testing, or records disclosure, while not being cold or dismissive — maintaining the therapeutic relationship with the family
De-escalates an angry, frightened parent with empathy: validates her fear and love for her son before explaining the limits, so the boundary lands as care, not obstruction
Keeps the door open for Jacob: frames the practice as a safe, confidential place he can come, and enlists the mother as an ally in getting him there rather than an adversary

Safety-nets and follows up: how Jacob can access help, young-people’s drug and family-support services, what to do if genuine risk emerges (and when the practice would act), support/follow-up for the mother, and clear documentation of the third-party contact

worked.txt: "I can hear how frightened and upset you are, and that comes from loving him — finding that in his room must have been a horrible shock. I really want to help you and Jacob. Let me be honest with you about what I can and can’t do, and then let’s find what actually works."

"Here’s the difficult bit. Jacob’s 16, and the law treats him as able to make his own health decisions — at 16 he can consent to his own treatment, and his right to confidentiality is the same as an adult’s — which means I can’t share what’s in his records, can’t call him in and drug-test him without his agreement, and can’t treat him when he’s not here and doesn’t know we’re speaking. I know that’s not what you hoped to hear. The reason matters though: that confidentiality is exactly what makes teenagers willing to come to us for help at all."

"Let me ask some things, because if Jacob were genuinely at risk that would change what I can do. Is this the first you’ve seen, or is it escalating? Any other drugs, any older people leading him, money or phones you can’t account for, big changes in his mood or sleep? … That helps me understand how worried to be."

"Here’s what I CAN do, and it’s genuinely useful. I can tell you about cannabis and young people so you’re informed. I can make it really easy for Jacob to come and talk to us himself, confidentially — often that lands far better than being marched in. And there are brilliant young-people’s drug services and parenting supports I’ll point you to. Scaring him straight tends to backfire; a calm, open door tends to work."

"Can I gently ask how YOU are in all this? You mentioned the divorce — it sounds like a lot has landed on you at once, and it’s easy to feel you’re losing your grip or somehow failing him. You’re not. The fact you rang says the opposite. Are you getting any support yourself?"

"So: I’ll text you the young-people’s drug service and a parenting line, and how Jacob can book his own confidential appointment. Try, if you can, to talk to him calmly rather than as a confrontation — ‘I’m worried, I’m here’ opens more doors than a row. If you ever see signs he’s in real danger — other drugs, threats, someone exploiting him, harm to himself — ring us and we WILL act. And I’d like to check in on how you’re doing too. You’re not failing him; you’re fighting for him."

f.learning: A parent ringing about an absent, competent 16-year-old is fundamentally a confidentiality-and-consent station. You cannot disclose a 16-year-old’s records, assess/treat or drug-test him on a parent’s demand, or act without his consent (at 16 consent rests on the Family Law Reform Act 1969, s8, and capacity is presumed under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 — Gillick is for under-16s and Fraser only for contraception; GMC 0–18 years and GMC Confidentiality 2017 govern disclosure), and you should neither confirm nor deny what he has discussed with the practice — and the reason matters: confidentiality is what keeps young people engaging with services. The skill is to hold that boundary kindly, after validating the parent’s fear and love, so it lands as care rather than obstruction. Then do what you CAN: a proportionate risk/safeguarding screen (escalation, other drugs, mental-health change, exploitation/county-lines, risk to self) that would change the calculus only if genuine risk emerges; general information; facilitating Jacob to attend confidentially himself; and signposting young-people’s drug and parenting/family services. The examinable hidden agenda is that "fix my son" masks the mother’s own crisis — a recent divorce, a sense of failing and losing control, possibly her own low mood — and the caller in front of you needs support in her own right. Decline harmful demands (covert testing, "scare him straight", records disclosure) without coldness, keep the door open for Jacob, and safety-net both of them.

knowledge.guideline: GMC 0–18 years (2007, updated 2018) · GMC Confidentiality (2017) · Family Law Reform Act 1969 s8 and Mental Capacity Act 2005 · Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026 (DfE) · NICE NG64 (drug misuse prevention, 2017)
knowledge.summary: A 16-year-old has the same right to confidentiality as an adult. You cannot share his record, test him or treat him on his mother’s request. You can listen, screen for real risk, give general information, open a door for him, and support her.

points.t: At 16 a young person can consent to treatment (Family Law Reform Act 1969, s8) and is presumed to have capacity (Mental Capacity Act 2005). Gillick competence applies to under-16s, not to Jacob. A drug test or examination needs his consent.

GMC 0–18 years and GMC Confidentiality (2017): do not disclose a young person’s information to a parent without consent unless it is justified in the public interest or needed to protect him or others from a risk of death or serious harm. Do not confirm or deny what he has discussed with the practice.
You can listen to a parent’s concerns and give general, non-patient-specific information without breaching confidentiality. Record the call on his notes.

Escalating or daily use, other drugs, a change in mood or behaviour, unusual thoughts, school refusal, unexplained money, phones or older contacts (child criminal exploitation, county lines), self-harm. Genuine risk of significant harm makes it a safeguarding matter under Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026.

Offer Jacob a confidential appointment he books himself; signpost local young people’s drug and alcohol services and FRANK for information. NICE NG64 targets drug misuse prevention at young people most at risk and suggests skills training for families alongside.

points.h: The caller is a patient too
points.t: A demand to “fix him” often hides the parent’s own distress. Here: a recent divorce and a sense of losing control. Ask how she is, screen her mood, and offer her an appointment in her own right.

dg.d: Let her say everything first; acknowledged the shock before any boundary.
Home situation, the divorce, school, and her support and coping.
Explains that no test or examination can happen without Jacob’s consent; offers him a confidential appointment; screens the mother’s mood.
Experimental use versus escalating use, exploitation, or a mental health change; the mother’s own low mood.
Other drugs, unexplained money or phones, older contacts, mood change, unusual thoughts, self-harm.
States that nothing reported meets a safeguarding threshold today, and names what would change that.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Confidentiality held kindly; general information; FRANK and local young people’s service; a calm conversation plan; a door open for Jacob.
Addresses the divorce and the mother’s low mood with an appointment for her.
Named triggers to ring back, 999 for immediate danger, documentation of the third-party call.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “you have to fix this” and “I feel like I’m losing him”, and explored her distress.
Idea (a parent can see his records and have him tested); concern (losing him, failing as a parent); expectation (test him, scare him).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — "I'm terrified he's going down a bad road and I've lost control of him." Underneath (only if asked about you): since the divorce you feel you are failing as a parent and you are struggling yourself — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, it’s Dr Lee from the surgery. I understand you’re calling about your son, Jacob. Tell me what’s happened.
model.why: Open question; lets her vent before any boundary

model.text: I found a bag of cannabis in his room this morning. I want you to get him in and drug-test him. And I want to know what he’s been telling you, because I’m his mother and I have a right to know. You have to fix this.

That must have been a horrible shock, and I can hear how worried you are about him. I do want to help you both. Can I ask a few things first, then be honest about what I can and can’t do, and then work out a plan together?
Fine. But I want something done.
Is this the first sign you’ve had, or have you been worried about him for a while?
model.why: Starts the risk screen with the timeline

model.text: He’s been moody and staying out late. But this is the first time I’ve found anything.
Have you noticed anything else, like other drugs, money or phones you can’t account for, or older people he’s spending time with that you don’t know?
No. Nothing like that. Just the bag. And he’s grumpy.
And how is he in himself? Going to school, sleeping, eating? Has he ever said anything that made you worry he might hurt himself, or said anything strange or out of character?
model.why: Screens for mental health change and risk to self

model.text: He goes to school. He eats. He hasn’t said anything like that.

Thank you, that helps. Here’s the hard part. At 16 the law treats Jacob as able to make his own health decisions. That means I can’t share anything from his records, even whether he’s been in, and I can’t call him in for a drug test without his agreement.
model.why: Explains the confidentiality and consent boundary clearly

model.text: That’s ridiculous. I’m his mother.

I understand why it feels that way. The reason matters, though. If teenagers thought we’d tell their parents, most wouldn’t come to us at all, including when they’re in real trouble. That privacy is what keeps the door open for him.
model.why: Gives the reason so the boundary lands as care

model.text: What I can say is this: if I ever had reason to think he was at serious risk, that would change what I can do. From what you’ve told me, that doesn’t sound like where things are today.
model.why: Names the safeguarding exception and what would trigger it

model.text: Can I ask how you are in all this? You sound like you’ve got a lot on your shoulders.
model.why: Turns to the caller’s own needs

model.text: (Pause.) I’ve just been through a divorce. It’s been awful. And now I feel like I’m losing him too. Like I’m failing.

That’s a lot to carry on your own. Finding that bag must have felt like proof of everything you were afraid of. But ringing today tells me you’re a mother fighting for her son, not failing him. How has your own mood been, and your sleep?
model.why: Validates, reframes, and screens her mood

model.text: Not great. I don’t sleep. I cry a lot.
I’d like to see you properly about that, in your own right. Would you book an appointment with me this week?
model.why: Offers care to the caller as a patient

model.text: Maybe. Yes. But what do I do about Jacob?

Here’s what I can do. I can tell you about cannabis and young people in general, and send you the local young people’s drug service and FRANK, which has good information for parents. And I can make it really easy for Jacob to come and talk to us himself, in confidence.
model.why: Turns the refused demands into what can be done

model.text: So I shouldn’t scare him straight?

Shouting or threats usually push young people away. A calm conversation tends to work better: “I found this, I’m worried, I’m not going anywhere, and you can talk to the GP on your own if you’d rather.” Would you be willing to try that?
model.why: Enlists her as an ally and negotiates one step

model.text: I can try. When he’s calmer.

If you see signs he’s in real danger, like harder drugs, threats, someone using him to carry things, or talk of hurting himself, ring us straight away and we will act. If he is ever in immediate danger, call 999. I’ll note this call on his record.
model.why: Specific triggers and a clear statement of when the practice would act

model.text: Just so I know I’ve explained it well, what will you do when you get off the phone?
Look at the links you send, talk to him calmly, tell him he can see you on his own. And book in for me.
That’s it exactly. You’re not on your own with this. Anything else before we finish?
No. Thank you. I’m sorry I shouted.

social.t: A recent divorce and a teenager pulling away. Her distress drives the anger; addressing it helps both of them.
Experimental use is common. Escalation, other drugs, falling school attendance or a change in mental state are what raise concern.

legal.t: Family Law Reform Act 1969, s8: a 16-year-old can consent to medical treatment. Mental Capacity Act 2005: presumed to have capacity. Testing without consent would be an assault.

GMC Confidentiality (2017) and GMC 0–18 years: disclosure without consent only where justified in the public interest or needed to protect him or others from serious harm, and usually after telling him.
Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026 (DfE): signs of child criminal exploitation or county lines, or other risk of significant harm, mean a referral to children’s social care.

professional.t: Record the third-party call on Jacob’s notes: who rang, what was said, the risk screen, the advice given and that no information was disclosed.
The mother is also a patient. Offer her an appointment in her own right; do not blur the two records.

community.t: FRANK (national drugs information and helpline); local young people’s drug and alcohol service; parenting and family support; relationship support after separation.

redFlags: Other drugs, dealing, unexplained money or phones, older controlling contacts (exploitation)
Change in mental state, unusual beliefs, self-harm or suicidal talk
Stopping school, going missing, violence at home
psychosocial: Recent divorce and its effect on her and on Jacob
How she and Jacob communicate at the moment
ice: Idea: as his mother she can see his records and have him tested
Concern: she is losing him and failing as a parent
Expectation: the GP will test him, tell her everything and scare him straight

playbook.diagnosis: “From what you’ve told me, nothing suggests Jacob is in immediate danger today. That could change, and if it did, we would act.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Confidentiality is like a door we keep open for teenagers. If they think we’ll tell their parents, they stop coming, even when they really need help. Keeping it private is how we keep Jacob safe in the long run.”

management.reflectIce: “You want to protect him, and it feels like you’re losing him. That comes through loud and clear. Let’s put that energy where it will actually help.”
management.psychosocial: Offer the mother her own appointment for her mood and the effects of the divorce; signpost parenting and relationship support.
sharedPlan: Hold confidentiality; no test or appointment without Jacob’s consent
General cannabis information, FRANK and the local young people’s service
A calm conversation at home and an open invitation for Jacob to book in himself
safetyNet: Ring the practice if signs of exploitation, other drugs, or self-harm appear; 999 if immediate danger
Document the call; follow up the mother at her appointment

pitfalls.intro: This is a confidentiality station dressed as a drug problem. Candidates fail by giving in to the demand, by refusing coldly, or by forgetting that the angry caller needs care too.

items.fail: Agreeing to call Jacob in for a drug test, or confirming whether he has been seen.
items.why: “Did not respect confidentiality or consent.” A competent 16-year-old’s information and body are his own.
items.fix: Explain that you can’t share or test without his consent, and why, then say what you can do.

items.fail: Opening with the rules: “I can’t discuss another patient.”
items.why: “Did not respond to the patient’s emotions.” The boundary then feels like a door slammed shut.
items.fix: Validate first: “That must have been a horrible shock.” Then set out the limits.

items.fail: No questions about risk because “it’s only cannabis”.
items.why: Exploitation, other drugs or a mental health change would change the safeguarding picture.
items.fix: Ask about other drugs, money, phones, older contacts, mood, school and self-harm.

items.why: Gillick applies to under-16s. At 16, consent rests on the Family Law Reform Act 1969 and the Mental Capacity Act 2005.
items.fix: “At 16 the law treats him as able to make his own health decisions.”

items.fail: Never asking how the mother is, so the divorce and her low mood stay hidden.
items.why: The hidden agenda is hers. Missing it loses the ICE and Relating marks.
items.fix: “How are you in all this?” Then offer her an appointment in her own right.

items.fail: Ending with “ring back if you’re worried”.
items.fix: Name the signs that would make you act, give 999 for immediate danger, and check she knows what she’ll do next.

Timeline, other drugs, money, phones, older contacts, mood, school, self-harm.
No records, no test, no treatment without his consent, and why. Name when the practice would act.

wordPics.fail: Shares or confirms record details, or agrees to call him in for a test; alternatively refuses coldly and ends the call; no risk screen; never asks about the mother.
wordPics.pass: Holds confidentiality and explains it; screens for risk; signposts services; offers Jacob a confidential appointment; basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: validates before the boundary so it lands as care; names what would trigger safeguarding action; uncovers the divorce and her low mood and offers her care; enlists her as an ally with a specific plan for a calm conversation; checks understanding.

avoid.dont: “I’m afraid I can’t discuss your son. Is there anything else?”
avoid.instead: “I can’t share his records, but I can listen, help you think it through, and make it easy for him to see us.”
avoid.why: A bare refusal holds the law but loses the relationship and the Relating marks.

avoid.dont: “He hasn’t been in to see us about drugs, if that helps.”
avoid.instead: “I can’t say whether he has or hasn’t been in. That applies to every young person here.”
avoid.why: Confirming or denying contact is itself a disclosure.

avoid.dont: “Bring him in and I’ll have a word with him about the dangers.”
avoid.instead: “He can book in himself, in confidence. That tends to go much better than being brought in.”
avoid.why: A consultation arranged to scare a competent 16-year-old is not consented care and usually backfires.

SCA_MODELS.text: So I shouldn’t scare him straight?

Shouting or threats usually push young people away. A calm conversation tends to work better: “I found this, I’m worried, I’m not going anywhere, and you can talk to the GP on your own if you’d rather.” Would you be willing to try that?
SCA_MODELS.why: Enlists her as an ally and negotiates one step

SCA_MODELS.text: I can try. When he’s calmer.

If you see signs he’s in real danger, like harder drugs, threats, someone using him to carry things, or talk of hurting himself, ring us straight away and we will act. If he is ever in immediate danger, call 999. I’ll note this call on his record.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific triggers and a clear statement of when the practice would act

SCA_MODELS.text: Just so I know I’ve explained it well, what will you do when you get off the phone?
Look at the links you send, talk to him calmly, tell him he can see you on his own. And book in for me.
That’s it exactly. You’re not on your own with this. Anything else before we finish?
No. Thank you. I’m sorry I shouted.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: GMC 0–18 years (2007, updated 2018) · GMC Confidentiality (2017) · Family Law Reform Act 1969 s8 and Mental Capacity Act 2005 · Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026 (DfE) · NICE NG64 (drug misuse prevention, 2017)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A 16-year-old has the same right to confidentiality as an adult. You cannot share his record, test him or treat him on his mother’s request. You can listen, screen for real risk, give general information, open a door for him, and support her.

points.t: At 16 a young person can consent to treatment (Family Law Reform Act 1969, s8) and is presumed to have capacity (Mental Capacity Act 2005). Gillick competence applies to under-16s, not to Jacob. A drug test or examination needs his consent.

GMC 0–18 years and GMC Confidentiality (2017): do not disclose a young person’s information to a parent without consent unless it is justified in the public interest or needed to protect him or others from a risk of death or serious harm. Do not confirm or deny what he has discussed with the practice.
You can listen to a parent’s concerns and give general, non-patient-specific information without breaching confidentiality. Record the call on his notes.

Escalating or daily use, other drugs, a change in mood or behaviour, unusual thoughts, school refusal, unexplained money, phones or older contacts (child criminal exploitation, county lines), self-harm. Genuine risk of significant harm makes it a safeguarding matter under Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026.

Offer Jacob a confidential appointment he books himself; signpost local young people’s drug and alcohol services and FRANK for information. NICE NG64 targets drug misuse prevention at young people most at risk and suggests skills training for families alongside.

points.h: The caller is a patient too
points.t: A demand to “fix him” often hides the parent’s own distress. Here: a recent divorce and a sense of losing control. Ask how she is, screen her mood, and offer her an appointment in her own right.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Let her say everything first; acknowledged the shock before any boundary.
Home situation, the divorce, school, and her support and coping.
Picked up “you have to fix this” and “I feel like I’m losing him”, and explored her distress.
Idea (a parent can see his records and have him tested); concern (losing him, failing as a parent); expectation (test him, scare him).
Explains that no test or examination can happen without Jacob’s consent; offers him a confidential appointment; screens the mother’s mood.
Experimental use versus escalating use, exploitation, or a mental health change; the mother’s own low mood.
Other drugs, unexplained money or phones, older contacts, mood change, unusual thoughts, self-harm.
States that nothing reported meets a safeguarding threshold today, and names what would change that.
Confidentiality held kindly; general information; FRANK and local young people’s service; a calm conversation plan; a door open for Jacob.
Addresses the divorce and the mother’s low mood with an appointment for her.
Named triggers to ring back, 999 for immediate danger, documentation of the third-party call.

social.t: A recent divorce and a teenager pulling away. Her distress drives the anger; addressing it helps both of them.
Experimental use is common. Escalation, other drugs, falling school attendance or a change in mental state are what raise concern.

legal.t: Family Law Reform Act 1969, s8: a 16-year-old can consent to medical treatment. Mental Capacity Act 2005: presumed to have capacity. Testing without consent would be an assault.

GMC Confidentiality (2017) and GMC 0–18 years: disclosure without consent only where justified in the public interest or needed to protect him or others from serious harm, and usually after telling him.
Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026 (DfE): signs of child criminal exploitation or county lines, or other risk of significant harm, mean a referral to children’s social care.

professional.t: Record the third-party call on Jacob’s notes: who rang, what was said, the risk screen, the advice given and that no information was disclosed.
The mother is also a patient. Offer her an appointment in her own right; do not blur the two records.

community.t: FRANK (national drugs information and helpline); local young people’s drug and alcohol service; parenting and family support; relationship support after separation.

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Confidentiality is like a door we keep open for teenagers. If they think we’ll tell their parents, they stop coming, even when they really need help. Keeping it private is how we keep Jacob safe in the long run.”

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This is a confidentiality station dressed as a drug problem. Candidates fail by giving in to the demand, by refusing coldly, or by forgetting that the angry caller needs care too.

items.fail: Agreeing to call Jacob in for a drug test, or confirming whether he has been seen.
items.why: “Did not respect confidentiality or consent.” A competent 16-year-old’s information and body are his own.
items.fix: Explain that you can’t share or test without his consent, and why, then say what you can do.

items.fail: Opening with the rules: “I can’t discuss another patient.”
items.why: “Did not respond to the patient’s emotions.” The boundary then feels like a door slammed shut.
items.fix: Validate first: “That must have been a horrible shock.” Then set out the limits.

items.fail: No questions about risk because “it’s only cannabis”.
items.why: Exploitation, other drugs or a mental health change would change the safeguarding picture.
items.fix: Ask about other drugs, money, phones, older contacts, mood, school and self-harm.

items.why: Gillick applies to under-16s. At 16, consent rests on the Family Law Reform Act 1969 and the Mental Capacity Act 2005.
items.fix: “At 16 the law treats him as able to make his own health decisions.”

items.fail: Never asking how the mother is, so the divorce and her low mood stay hidden.
items.why: The hidden agenda is hers. Missing it loses the ICE and Relating marks.
items.fix: “How are you in all this?” Then offer her an appointment in her own right.

items.fail: Ending with “ring back if you’re worried”.
items.fix: Name the signs that would make you act, give 999 for immediate danger, and check she knows what she’ll do next.
